proposal: The Mandate recommends strengthening the SBA Office of Advocacy: amend the Regulatory Flexibility Act so agencies send proposed rules and initial analyses to Advocacy 60 days before publication and respond to its comments, count indirect costs in RFA analysis, direct agencies to comply with the Act (as in 2017 executive orders), hold regional roundtables, and raise Advocacy's budget by at least 50 percent (about $4.6 million). It also suggests Congress presumptively exempt small businesses from new rules unless Advocacy signs off.

status_summary: None of the Mandate's specific Office of Advocacy recommendations is in effect, though some have been requested or introduced. On budget, an appendix to Advocacy's FY2026 budget justification (posted March 2026) requests $14.2 million, about $4 million above baseline, and the administration's FY2027 request raises Advocacy from $10.1 million to $14.1 million (CRS), roughly a 40 percent increase against the Mandate's 50 percent; Congress provided $10.1 million for FY2026. The Prove It Act (S. 495 and H.R. 1163, introduced 2025-02-10) would count indirect costs in RFA analysis and let Advocacy review no-impact certifications; it has not passed either chamber, and no bill adopting the Mandate's 60-day pre-publication review or presumptive small business exemption was found. No directive specifically requiring agencies to comply with the Regulatory Flexibility Act was found; Executive Order 14219 (2025-02-19) tells agencies to identify regulations that burden small business but does not mention the Act or Advocacy. Casey Mulligan was confirmed as Chief Counsel for Advocacy on 2025-08-01 (52 to 44), released a report on Biden-era rules certified under the Act on his first day, and told the House Small Business Committee on 2026-01-07 that Advocacy's regional team had visited at least 40 states (his statements); the budget appendix treats a return to the Regional Deregulatory Roundtable initiative as competing with other priorities at current funding. Advocacy's leadership page, viewed 2026-10-07, lists an Acting Chief Counsel; the reason was not found.

timeline.event: Sen. Ernst introduces the Prove It Act (S. 495): indirect costs in initial regulatory flexibility analyses, a petition process for Advocacy review of no-impact certifications, and a rule-nonapplication penalty for agencies that do not take part. A House version, H.R. 1163 (Rep. Finstad), was introduced the same day.

Executive Order 14219 signed (published 2025-02-25): agencies are to identify regulations in seven classes, including those placing undue burdens on small business, and report them to OIRA within 60 days. It does not refer to the Regulatory Flexibility Act or Advocacy.
Senate confirms Casey Mulligan as Chief Counsel for Advocacy by a vote of 52 to 44, per Sen. Ernst's release; the Senate Small Business Committee had reported the nomination on 2025-04-02 by 10 to 9.

Advocacy reports that on his first day the Chief Counsel sent the President and Congress a report on more than 12,000 Biden-era rules certified under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, which it says found many certifications improperly made.

Chief Counsel Mulligan testifies to the House Small Business Committee: cites EO 14192 and EO 14219, reports a regional advocacy team with visits to at least 40 states, asks Congress to support the President's budget, and lists options such as barring certification of major rules without his approval and considering the Prove It Act.

Advocacy posts an appendix to its FY2026 budget justification (upload month March 2026; day not confirmed) describing a requested budget of $14.2 million, an increase of $4 million, to expand legal and economic staff, communications and travel to hear from small businesses.

CRS reports the administration's FY2027 request raises the Office of Advocacy from $10.1 million in FY2026 to $14.1 million, the one major increase in an SBA request that otherwise falls 74.7 percent.
Advocacy's leadership page (viewed on this date) names Everett M. Woodel, Jr. as Acting Chief Counsel and does not mention Mr. Mulligan; the reason was not found.

title: Strengthen the Office of Advocacy's regulatory review role and budget
uncertainties: Advocacy's two FY2026 budget documents conflict: the July 2025 justification reviewed earlier shows a $10.211 million request (flat) and 55 FTE, while the appendix posted in March 2026 describes a $14.2 million FY2026 request; the difference was not reconciled, and the $10.1 million FY2026 enacted figure comes from the CRS Insight. The CRS Insight, not the FY2027 budget document itself, was read. Mulligan's testimony is his own account and says it does not necessarily reflect the Administration's views; its figures (60 agencies, 40 states, 300 issues) are unverified. Why the leadership page lists an Acting Chief Counsel after a September 2025 to January 2026 period in which Mulligan was in office was not found (possible departure, or an outdated page). A bill tracker shows H.R. 1163 on the House Union Calendar (No. 552, last action 2026-05-04) with 30 cosponsors, which implies a committee report, but the tracker also says no markup is recorded; not confirmed at congress.gov.
